prompt: A square-and-multiply implementation processes every bit of a non-negative exponent. Why can it handle a huge exponent with relatively few modular multiplications?

options.text: It loops once for every integer below the exponent.
options.explanation: That is the impractical repeated-multiplication approach.

options.text: It squares once per bit and multiplies into the result only when that bit is set.
options.explanation: Work tracks representation length instead of the exponent’s numeric value.

options.text: A modular multiplication costs constant time on every possible operand size.
options.explanation: Operation count and bit cost are distinct; larger moduli require more arithmetic work.

options.text: Its bit-dependent branches automatically make it constant-time cryptographic code.
options.explanation: Those branches can reveal information about secret exponent bits.

workedExample: Repeated squaring supplies the base raised to successively doubled powers. A set bit includes the corresponding power in the result. Each exponent bit therefore needs only a bounded number of modular multiplications. Reducing keeps residues bounded by the modulus, but timing still depends on implementation and operand size.
